newsitem.title: UK: Paisley attacks Hume plan for N.Ireland marches.
newsitem.headline: Paisley attacks Hume plan for N.Ireland marches.

text.p: A prominent pro-British politician in Northern Ireland said on Monday that nothing good would come of talks intended to defuse tension over a protestant parade that has proved a flashpoint for civil unrest.

Democratic Unionist Party leader Ian Paisley said talks announced on Sunday by Nobel peace prize nominee John Hume would simply follow an agenda set by the guerrilla Irish Republican Army, fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland.
The talks aim to calm tension building over a Protestant Orange Order parade in July which last year sparked the worst civil unrest in Northern Ireland for decades.

Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), said that he and the Grand Master of the Orange Order, Robert Saulters, would hold talks with the residents of Garvaghy Road, the flashpoint for last year's violence.
"I don't think anything good will come of talking to those that represent the IRA and represent the IRA agenda," Paisley told BBC radio.
"Anything that comes out of these negotiations will be capitulation to the IRA. It is an IRA agenda that will be followed at these talks"

The talks will be the first time that the Orange Order, whose Protestant members want Northern Ireland to stay British, have agreed to negotiate with Garvaghy Road residents -- Catholic Irish nationalists who identify with Dublin.
"This is a breakthrough and I look forward to all sides coming together. I hope all participants will approach this in a positive frame of mind," Hume said in a statement on Sunday.
Last July police banned the annual parade from the Protestant church at Drumcree down the Garvaghy Road area of the town of Portadown, but reversed the ban after province-wide rioting by Protestants.
The U-turn ignited Catholic anger instead and paralysed the province for a few days as barricades were thrown across highways and police attacked with petrol bombs and stones.

Hume's initative was announced as a tense standoff developed in the village of Dunloy, 50 miles (80 km) north of Belfast where a march by a Protestant order, the Apprentice Boys, was stopped by a protest from Catholic village residents.
Catholics, a 40 percent minority in Northern Ireland, say such parades celebrate centuries-old Protestant victories over Catholics and are triumphalist and intimidatory.
But Protestants say they are a birthright and a harmless tradition which celebrates their British identity and Protestant faith and are not intended to offend anyone.
